Sources of support at home, at school, and among friends.
optionRationales: Correct. Substance use can affect thinking and is a key adolescent risk.
Correct. Injury can cause new cognitive changes.
Correct. Mood disorders and self-harm risk must be assessed in teens with new decline.
Incorrect. The teen’s own report is needed; parent opinions are secondary.
Correct. Support networks guide planning and safety.
questions.rationale: Adolescents’ self-control is still developing while peers and rewards pull hard, so a sudden drop in performance needs a nonjudgmental, private assessment. The nurse asks about substances, injury, mood, sleep, self-harm, and support. Relying on parents’ opinions is tempting because parents are present and concerned, but the teen’s own words are the most important data. A sudden drop, new psychotic signs, or self-harm risk needs action.
questions.takeaway: For teens with new decline, ask directly about substances, injury, mood, self-harm, and support.
questions.hintContent: Think about the most common reasons a teen’s thinking or performance changes quickly.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose topics the client can answer about himself or herself.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A client with major neurocognitive disorder is being discharged to live with her son, who works full time. Which actions should the nurse include in discharge planning? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the son about his work schedule and who will be with her during the day.
Watch the son set up her medicines and ask him to explain the schedule back.
Refer to social work for adult day programs or in-home help.
Assume the son can give all medicines because he is a family member.
Teach the son to correct her firmly whenever she is mistaken.
Teach the son to report a sudden change in alertness or confusion.
optionRationales: Correct. Caregiver time and availability must be assessed, not assumed.
Correct. Observing the caregiver’s skill confirms safe medicine management.
Correct. Team referrals support caregivers and match help to real needs.
Incorrect. Family ability, time, and understanding must be checked before relying on them.
Incorrect. Repeated correction raises distress; responding to feelings works better.
Correct. Families often notice delirium first and must know to report it.
questions.rationale: Discharge planning for a client with dementia depends on what the caregiver can actually do. The nurse assesses the son’s time, observes his skill with medicines, connects the family to team resources, and teaches him to report a sudden change. Assuming a family member can manage everything is tempting because it simplifies the plan, but time, skill, and understanding must be checked. Firm correction is not a recommended approach to dementia confusion.
questions.takeaway: Never assume family can provide care; assess their time, skill, and understanding.
questions.hintContent: Note the detail that the son works full time.
questions.hintStrategy: In discharge SATA items, choose options that verify support rather than assume it.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 62-year-old client with no psychiatric history is admitted for a hip fracture and on day 2 reports seeing people standing in the corner of the room. Which data should the nurse collect? Select all that apply.
options: All medicines started or stopped since admission.
Usual alcohol intake and the time of the last drink.
Temperature, pulse, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation.
Whether attention and alertness have changed since admission.
A family history of schizophrenia to confirm the diagnosis.
optionRationales: Correct. New medicines, such as opioids, can cause perceptual disturbances.
Correct. Withdrawal is a common cause of new hallucinations in the first days of a stay.
Correct. Vital signs may reveal infection, hypoxia, or withdrawal.
Correct. Inattention or altered alertness suggests delirium rather than a primary psychotic disorder.
Incorrect. Family history cannot confirm a diagnosis or explain a sudden new symptom during an acute illness.
questions.rationale: New hallucinations in a medically ill adult with no psychiatric history call for a search for medical causes. Medicines, substance withdrawal, infection, hypoxia, and delirium are common culprits, so the nurse gathers medication changes, alcohol history, vital signs, and changes in attention and alertness. Using family history to confirm schizophrenia is tempting because it sounds like a risk factor, but it cannot explain an acute change during hospitalization. One new symptom does not establish a psychiatric diagnosis.
questions.takeaway: New hallucinations during illness require a search for medical causes first.
questions.hintContent: Ask what could have changed in this client’s body since admission.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose assessments that look for reversible causes before psychiatric labels.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A nurse on a surgical unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A 70-year-old after knee replacement resting with pain 3 of 10 who conversed at the last check.
A 60-year-old after appendectomy who repeatedly asks when discharge will be.
A 78-year-old with dementia who asks the same question as on prior days.
An 85-year-old after hip repair who slept through lunch and drifts off mid-answer.
optionRationales: Incorrect. A comfortable client who is conversing at baseline is stable.
Incorrect. Repeated questions about discharge reflect anxiety, not an acute change.
Incorrect. A behavior that matches her known baseline is not a new change.
Correct. Drowsiness and inattention that are new suggest hypoactive delirium, which is easy to miss.
questions.rationale: Hypoactive delirium is quiet and easy to miss, but quiet does not mean stable. An older adult after hip surgery who sleeps through meals and drifts off mid-answer shows reduced alertness and inattention, which may reflect hypoxia, drug effects, infection, or another acute cause. The client with dementia is tempting because she is confused, but her behavior matches her baseline. The anxious and comfortable clients are stable.
questions.takeaway: Quiet, drowsy, inattentive clients may have hypoactive delirium and need prompt assessment.
questions.hintContent: Look past who is loudest and find whose alertness has changed.
questions.hintStrategy: In priority items, quiet changes in alertness can be more dangerous than repetitive behavior.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: At 0200, an 86-year-old client being treated for a urinary infection and delirium is restless and calling out. The client has a PRN order for lorazepam for sleep and is not withdrawing from alcohol. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give the PRN lorazepam so the client can sleep through the night.
Assess for pain, a full bladder, and oxygenation before any medicine.
Apply mitts to the hands so the client cannot pull at tubes.
Call the family and ask someone to come sit with the client now.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium in older adults and do not treat the cause.
Correct. Restlessness may come from fixable triggers, so the nurse assesses causes first.
Incorrect. Restraint devices are not the first step and can increase agitation.
Incorrect. Family presence can help later, but the cause of restlessness must be assessed first.
questions.rationale: Restlessness in delirium is often a signal of a physical need, such as pain, a full bladder, or low oxygen. The nurse assesses these causes before considering any medication. Giving the lorazepam is tempting because the order exists and the client cannot sleep, but benzodiazepines can cause or worsen delirium in older adults and are generally reserved for specific uses such as withdrawal. The order itself should be clarified with the prescriber.
questions.takeaway: Assess causes of restlessness before using sedatives, and question benzodiazepines in older adults.
questions.hintContent: Think about what bodily needs could make a confused client restless at night.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose assessment over medication or restraint when the cause is unknown.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: In the post-anesthesia care unit, a 5-year-old who had a tonsillectomy is thrashing, crying inconsolably, and does not seem to recognize his mother. She says, “He’s just being bratty.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the mother to hold him firmly in her lap until he calms down.
Protect him from injury and assess his airway, oxygen, and pain.
Tell the mother this behavior is normal and will pass soon.
Set firm limits and explain that crying slows his recovery.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Holding him does not address possible airway, oxygen, or pain problems.
Correct. Children may have delirium after anesthesia, and safety plus physical assessment come first.
Incorrect. Reassurance without assessment could miss hypoxia, bleeding, or pain.
Incorrect. Treating an altered mental state as defiance is inappropriate.
questions.rationale: Children may act very differently during severe illness or after anesthesia, and this should not be called defiance. Not recognizing a parent and inconsolable thrashing suggest a change in awareness that requires protection from injury and assessment of airway, oxygenation, and pain. After a tonsillectomy, airway and bleeding are especially important. Reassuring the mother is tempting because emergence behavior is common, but the nurse must assess before assuming it is benign.
questions.takeaway: In children, treat a new change in awareness after anesthesia as a physical concern, not misbehavior.
questions.hintContent: Consider what could be physically wrong in a child just out of surgery.
questions.hintStrategy: When a caregiver blames behavior, choose safety and physical assessment first.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation

questions.stem: Seven hours after her urinary catheter was removed, a 79-year-old client after abdominal surgery has become newly restless and keeps trying to get out of bed. She has not voided and her lower abdomen feels firm. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Request an order for a sedative to manage the restlessness.
Encourage her to drink more fluids to help her void.
Reorient her to the room and dim the lights to calm her.
Assess the bladder with a bladder scanner or as per protocol.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sedation masks a likely physical cause and can worsen delirium.
Incorrect. Adding fluid to an overdistended bladder does not relieve retention.
Incorrect. Reorientation alone ignores the likely cause of the new restlessness.
Correct. No voiding and a firm lower abdomen suggest urinary retention, a common delirium trigger.
questions.rationale: Urinary retention is a common, fixable trigger of delirium, especially after catheter removal. This client has not voided in seven hours, has a firm lower abdomen, and is newly restless. Assessing bladder volume lets the nurse confirm retention and follow the protocol or notify the provider. Encouraging fluids is tempting because it seems to promote voiding, but it adds volume to a bladder that may already be overdistended.
questions.takeaway: In new restlessness after catheter removal, assess for urinary retention.
questions.hintContent: Link the time since catheter removal to her abdominal finding.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for a specific physical trigger in the stem before choosing calming or sedating actions.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client admitted with pneumonia has become newly confused and is picking at the sheets. Respirations are 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply oxygen as ordered or per protocol and raise the head of the bed.
Complete a delirium screen to confirm the change in thinking.
Request an antipsychotic for the agitation from the provider.
Call the family to ask about the client’s usual mental status.
optionRationales: Correct. Hypoxia is a direct cause of delirium and must be corrected immediately.
Incorrect. Screening does not treat the low oxygen that is likely causing the change.
Incorrect. Antipsychotics do not correct hypoxia, the likely cause.
Incorrect. Baseline history can wait until oxygenation is addressed.
questions.rationale: Low oxygen is a common and dangerous cause of delirium. With an oxygen saturation of 86% and rapid breathing, the nurse’s first action is to improve oxygenation and positioning, then notify the provider. A delirium screen is tempting because it documents the change, but it does nothing for the cause. Antipsychotics do not correct hypoxia, infection, or other physical triggers.
questions.takeaway: When delirium appears with low oxygen, treat the oxygen first.
questions.hintContent: Focus on the vital sign that is clearly abnormal.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply ABCs: a breathing problem comes before screening or sedation.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation

questions.stem: A client who is 32 weeks pregnant calls the clinic nurse line. Her husband reports that she has a bad headache and, over the past few hours, has been confused about where she is. He says, “I think it’s just pregnancy brain.” Which action by the nurse is best?
options: Tell him to let her rest and call back if she is not better tomorrow.
Have her seen emergently for blood pressure and mental status checks.
Recommend acetaminophen for the headache and recheck in 1 hour.
Reassure him that mild forgetfulness is common in late pregnancy.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Waiting delays evaluation of a possibly life-threatening problem.
Correct. New confusion during pregnancy can signal serious illness and needs urgent evaluation.
Incorrect. Treating the headache alone ignores the new confusion.
Incorrect. Mild forgetfulness is different from new disorientation, which is not expected.
questions.rationale: New confusion during pregnancy or after birth can signal serious illness, such as a hypertensive disorder, and needs urgent assessment of vital signs and mental status with prompt provider notification. A headache together with new disorientation is especially concerning. Reassuring the husband is tempting because mild forgetfulness can occur in pregnancy, but disorientation to place over hours is a different and dangerous finding. Waiting until tomorrow could allow a seizure or stroke.
questions.takeaway: New confusion in pregnancy is urgent until proven otherwise.
questions.hintContent: Distinguish mild forgetfulness from new disorientation.
questions.hintStrategy: When a family member offers a benign explanation, ask whether the finding is new and serious.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: An RN delegated care of a client with hypoactive delirium to an assistive personnel (AP). Which report from the AP requires the RN’s immediate attention?
options: “She ate half of her breakfast after I helped her sit up.”
“Her glasses and hearing aids have been on since 0800.”
“She is much harder to wake up than she was this morning.”
“She asked twice what day it was and calmed after I told her.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Partial intake with assistance is useful information but not urgent.
Incorrect. This shows prevention measures are in place.
Correct. A drop in alertness is a sign of worsening and needs RN assessment now.
Incorrect. Mild disorientation that responds to reminders is expected in delirium.
questions.rationale: In hypoactive delirium, a drop in alertness can signal oversedation, worsening hypoxia, or progression of the underlying cause. The AP was given a clear threshold to report if the client became harder to wake, and this report meets it. Asking what day it is twice is tempting to choose because it sounds like confusion, but it is expected in delirium and resolved with a simple reminder. Partial intake and sensory aids are routine data.
questions.takeaway: A client who is harder to wake needs immediate RN assessment.
questions.hintContent: Find the report that shows a decline from earlier today.
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation reports, choose the one that shows a change in alertness or safety.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: At 1900, a day-shift nurse prepares the handoff for a client with suspected delirium. Which information is most important to include?
options: The client prefers decaffeinated tea with breakfast each morning.
The client’s son visited this afternoon and will return tomorrow.
The client watched television for about an hour after lunch today.
Clear at 0900, drowsy and inattentive at 1500, and urine culture pending.
optionRationales: Incorrect. A preference is minor compared with the acute change in status.
Incorrect. Visitor plans are helpful but not the key safety information.
Incorrect. This activity does not describe attention or the change in status.
Correct. Fluctuation in mental status and pending results tell the next nurse what is new and what to follow.
questions.rationale: Delirium comes and goes, so the next nurse may see a client who seems clear and miss the earlier change. Handoff should include specific times, observed behaviors, and pending workup so the trend can be followed. Visitor plans and preferences are tempting because they support person-centered care, but they do not protect the client from a missed decline. Concrete, time-stamped findings are the most important part of the report.
questions.takeaway: Hand off delirium with time-stamped changes and pending results.
questions.hintContent: Ask what the next nurse needs to recognize a fluctuating problem.
questions.hintStrategy: In handoff items, choose the information that affects safety and follow-up.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A night-shift nurse in long-term care is told that a resident with dementia “always sundowns.” Tonight she is more confused than usual, is warm to the touch, and dozes off in the middle of sentences. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document the behavior as her usual evening sundowning pattern.
Turn on the television to distract her until she settles down.
Assess vital signs and look for an acute cause of the change.
Give her the usual evening snack and help her back to bed.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sundowning describes timing only and does not explain new fever and drowsiness.
Incorrect. Distraction ignores signs of a possible acute illness.
Correct. Fever and new drowsiness suggest delirium from an acute cause that needs assessment.
Incorrect. Routine comfort measures do not address a new physical change.
questions.rationale: Sundowning only describes worsening confusion in the evening; it does not explain why. This resident has new findings that go beyond her usual pattern: warmth and drifting off mid-sentence. These suggest delirium from an acute cause such as infection, so the nurse assesses vital signs and looks for the cause. Charting the usual pattern is tempting because staff expect evening confusion, but it misses a new, possibly serious change.
questions.takeaway: Sundowning is a timing word, not an explanation; new physical signs need assessment.
questions.hintContent: Separate what is usual for this resident from what is new tonight.
questions.hintStrategy: When a label offers an easy explanation, check for new physical findings first.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation

questions.stem: A trained nurse completes the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) for an 80-year-old client on day 3 after a bowel resection. The findings are shown in the exhibit. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The screen is negative because the client’s thinking is organized.
The screen is positive and the client needs prompt clinical evaluation.
The screen is incomplete because all four features must be present.
The findings suggest dementia because the client is still oriented to name.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Organized thinking does not make the screen negative when altered consciousness is present.
Correct. Acute change and inattention, plus altered consciousness, meet the classic CAM pattern.
Incorrect. The pattern requires features 1 and 2 plus either 3 or 4, not all four.
Incorrect. Orientation to name does not exclude delirium, and the acute change argues against dementia alone.
questions.rationale: The CAM looks for an acute onset or fluctuating course plus inattention, together with either disorganized thinking or an altered level of consciousness. This client has a sudden change, misses several letters on an attention task, and is lethargic, which meets the pattern even though thinking is organized. Calling the screen negative is tempting because one feature is absent, but only one of features 3 or 4 is needed. A positive screen calls for clinical evaluation of causes.
questions.takeaway: CAM needs acute change and inattention, plus either disorganized thinking or altered alertness.
questions.hintContent: Check which features are required and which are “either-or.”
questions.hintStrategy: For tool-interpretation items, apply the rule exactly as written to the data in the exhibit.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

Absent: answers are logical and on topic
Present: lethargic, drifts off between questions

questions.stem: At 1400, a nurse finds a postoperative client drowsy and unable to stay with a simple question. At 1600, the client is alert and the nurse’s CAM screen is negative. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Conclude delirium has been ruled out and stop further screening.
Chart that the 1400 finding was an error in the nurse’s assessment.
Report the 1400 change and reassess attention through the shift.
Wait until the client is drowsy again before notifying anyone.
optionRationales: Incorrect. A single negative screen does not erase a decline the nurse already observed.
Incorrect. The earlier observation was real data and should not be dismissed.
Correct. Delirium fluctuates, so the observed change is reported and reassessment continues.
Incorrect. Waiting for another episode delays evaluation of an already observed change.
questions.rationale: Delirium comes and goes, so a short interaction can miss it. A negative screen does not erase a decline the nurse observed earlier, and fluctuation itself is a key feature. The nurse reports the earlier change and continues to reassess attention over time. Concluding that delirium is ruled out is tempting because the screen was negative, but that ignores the most important clue: the change at 1400.
questions.takeaway: A negative screen does not erase an observed change; fluctuation is a feature of delirium.
questions.hintContent: Ask what makes delirium hard to catch in a single assessment.
questions.hintStrategy: When data conflict over time, choose the option that reports and continues to reassess.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: The daughter of an 83-year-old client with new delirium says, “She always gets confused when she has a bladder infection. Can’t you just start her antibiotics?” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Yes, confusion in older adults almost always means a bladder infection.”
“Antibiotics are not needed because infections rarely cause confusion.”
“The provider will decide later; please do not worry about the cause.”
“Infection is possible, but the team will also look for other causes.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Confusion alone does not prove a urinary infection.
Incorrect. Infection is a common cause of delirium, so this is inaccurate.
Incorrect. This dismisses her concern and offers no explanation.
Correct. Delirium often has several causes, so the team checks more than one before treating.
questions.rationale: New confusion can come from infection, low oxygen, dehydration, medicines, retention, pain, and other triggers, often several at once. Confusion alone does not prove a urinary infection, and treating an assumed cause could miss the real problem. The nurse validates the daughter’s experience while explaining that the team looks for all possible triggers. Agreeing that confusion means infection is tempting because her history supports it, but it would stop the search too early.
questions.takeaway: New confusion does not prove infection; look for several possible causes.
questions.hintContent: Consider how many different triggers can cause delirium.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose a response that respects the family’s input while keeping the assessment open.
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity

questions.stem: A 76-year-old client on day 2 after a cardiac procedure tried to climb out of bed and pulled at the IV during the night. On day shift, the same client is withdrawn, answers slowly, and dozes off during meals. Which type of delirium do these findings describe?
options: Hyperactive delirium only, because the night behavior was agitated.
Hypoactive delirium only, because the day behavior is quiet.
Mixed delirium, because the client switches between both patterns.
Sundowning, because the agitation occurred mainly at night.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The day findings show reduced activity, so the picture is not hyperactive only.
Incorrect. The night findings show agitation, so the picture is not hypoactive only.
Correct. Switching between hyperactive and hypoactive signs is mixed delirium.
Incorrect. Sundowning describes timing only and does not explain the quiet day findings.
questions.rationale: Delirium can be hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed. Hyperactive delirium shows agitation and pulling at lines, hypoactive delirium shows withdrawal and drowsiness, and mixed delirium switches between them, sometimes in the same day. Sundowning is tempting because the agitation was at night, but it only describes timing and not the cause or pattern. Recognizing the quiet day phase as delirium prevents the team from calling it improvement.
questions.takeaway: A client who switches between agitation and withdrawal has mixed delirium.
questions.hintContent: Compare the night findings with the day findings.
questions.hintStrategy: When findings change over the day, consider a category that includes both patterns.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A nurse teaches the wife of a client who is being discharged after an episode of delirium. Which statement by the wife indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I’ll call the provider if he suddenly gets harder to wake or more confused.”
“Once he is home, his thinking will be back to normal within a day or two.”
“I’ll make sure his glasses and hearing aids are in every morning.”
“We’ll keep a regular routine, with daylight and activity during the day.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reporting a sudden change is correct.
Correct. Recovery time varies, and some clients take much longer to return toward baseline.
Incorrect. Sensory aids support orientation and are correct.
Incorrect. A normal day-night routine supports recovery.
questions.rationale: Delirium often improves as its causes are treated, but recovery time varies and some clients take weeks or longer to return toward baseline. The nurse should not promise a quick recovery, so the wife’s expectation of a return to normal in a day or two needs correction. The other statements reflect correct teaching about reporting changes, sensory aids, and routine. Reporting a sudden change may look like it needs teaching because it sounds alarming, but it is exactly what families should do.
questions.takeaway: Do not promise a quick return to baseline after delirium; recovery time varies.
questions.hintContent: Look for the statement that promises too much.
questions.hintStrategy: In “needs further teaching” items, find the statement that is inaccurate or overly certain.
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients admitted today. Which client is at highest risk for developing delirium?
options: A 45-year-old having elective knee arthroscopy with no medical history.
An 88-year-old with dementia and hearing loss having hip fracture surgery.
A 30-year-old with a simple ankle fracture who lives alone at home.
A 62-year-old having outpatient cataract surgery under local anesthesia.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Younger age and no risk factors make delirium less likely.
Correct. Older age, existing cognitive impairment, sensory loss, and major surgery combine to raise risk.
Incorrect. Living alone is not a major delirium risk in a healthy young adult.
Incorrect. A brief outpatient procedure in a younger client carries lower risk.
questions.rationale: Risk factors lower the brain’s reserve, and new triggers tip it into delirium. Older age, existing cognitive impairment, hearing or vision loss, severe illness, and major surgery all add to risk, and this 88-year-old has several at once. The cataract client is tempting because vision affects risk, but a brief outpatient procedure in a younger client is far less risky. Identifying high-risk clients early allows prevention measures to start on admission.
questions.takeaway: Stacked risk factors such as age, dementia, sensory loss, and major surgery mean the highest delirium risk.
questions.hintContent: Count each client’s risk factors.
questions.hintStrategy: For “highest risk” items, choose the client with the most combined risk factors.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client recovering from delirium sleeps much of the day and is awake and restless most of the night. Which intervention best helps restore a normal sleep-wake pattern?
options: Keep the room dark and quiet around the clock to promote rest.
Give PRN diphenhydramine at bedtime to help the client fall asleep.
Open blinds and promote activity by day; protect rest at night.
Allow naps whenever the client wishes throughout the day.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Constant darkness removes cues that help orientation and day-night rhythm.
Incorrect. Diphenhydramine is anticholinergic and can worsen delirium in older adults.
Correct. Daylight, activity, and protected night rest support a normal routine.
Incorrect. Unlimited daytime naps reinforce the reversed sleep pattern.
questions.rationale: Sleep-wake reversal is common in delirium. Daylight and activity during the day, plus protected rest at night, help restore the normal pattern and support orientation. Diphenhydramine is tempting because it is an easy sleep aid, but it is strongly anticholinergic and can worsen delirium in older adults. A dark room all day removes the cues the client needs to stay oriented.
questions.takeaway: Restore sleep with daytime light and activity and protected nighttime rest, not sedating sleep aids.
questions.hintContent: Think about what tells the brain whether it is day or night.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the nondrug intervention that targets the specific problem described.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort

questions.stem: A client with hyperactive delirium who remained severely distressed despite nondrug measures received short-term haloperidol as ordered. Which finding should the nurse report to the prescriber promptly?
options: Follows a one-step request and eats lunch after set-up.
Sleeps through the night and wakes at the usual time.
Speaks in a calmer voice when family members visit.
Develops new muscle stiffness and a shuffling gait.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Improved attention and function are positive responses.
Incorrect. A restored sleep-wake pattern is a desired outcome.
Incorrect. Reduced distress without oversedation is a desired effect.
Correct. New rigidity and shuffling suggest an extrapyramidal effect that requires prompt reporting.
questions.rationale: Haloperidol and similar drugs require monitoring for sedation, heart and nerve side effects, falls, and response. New muscle stiffness and a shuffling gait suggest extrapyramidal effects, which raise fall risk and need prompt reporting. A calmer voice might look like a concern if the nurse worries about sedation, but calm with preserved interaction is the intended effect. Recovery is judged by attention and function, and the other options show progress.
questions.takeaway: Monitor antipsychotics for nerve side effects such as rigidity and report them promptly.
questions.hintContent: Separate desired effects from new adverse movement findings.
questions.hintStrategy: In medication evaluation items, find the finding that signals harm rather than benefit.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the medication administration record shown in the exhibit for an 81-year-old client with Lewy body dementia who developed delirium after a fall. The client is not withdrawing from alcohol. Which orders should the nurse clarify with the prescriber before giving them? Select all that apply.
options: Diphenhydramine at bedtime as needed for sleep.
Lorazepam every 6 hours as needed for restlessness.
Haloperidol every 6 hours as needed for agitation.
Acetaminophen every 6 hours as needed for pain.
Polyethylene glycol daily for constipation.
optionRationales: Correct. Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and can worsen delirium in older adults.
Correct. Benzodiazepines can cause or worsen delirium and are usually reserved for uses such as withdrawal.
Correct. Haloperidol needs special caution in Lewy body dementia because of severe sensitivity reactions.
Incorrect. Pain control with acetaminophen is appropriate and can reduce delirium triggers.
Incorrect. Preventing constipation supports comfort and is appropriate.
questions.rationale: Some drugs can cause or worsen delirium, especially in older adults. Strongly anticholinergic drugs such as diphenhydramine and benzodiazepines such as lorazepam are two key groups, and haloperidol needs special caution in clients with Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia. Acetaminophen is tempting to question because it is a medication, but treating pain actually removes a delirium trigger. The nurse clarifies the risky orders before giving any of them.
questions.takeaway: Question diphenhydramine and benzodiazepines in older adults, and haloperidol in Lewy body or Parkinson disease.
questions.hintContent: Check each drug against the client’s age and the diagnosis listed in the stem.
questions.hintStrategy: For MAR SATA items, judge each order against the specific client, not the drug in general.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing older adults on a medical unit for hypoactive delirium. Which findings are consistent with hypoactive delirium when they are new for the client? Select all that apply.
options: Drifts off in the middle of answering a question.
Answers slowly and says little compared with yesterday.
Stops eating and shows no interest in usual activities.
Pulls at the IV line and tries to climb out of bed.
Rests with eyes closed but wakes easily and follows a conversation.
optionRationales: Correct. Falling asleep mid-conversation shows reduced alertness and inattention.
Correct. Slowed, reduced responses are typical of hypoactive delirium.
Correct. Withdrawal and reduced activity are hypoactive features that are often missed.
Incorrect. Agitation and pulling at lines are hyperactive features.
Incorrect. A client who wakes easily and follows conversation is resting, not delirious.
questions.rationale: Hypoactive delirium shows less activity: withdrawal, slow answers, drowsiness, and drifting off mid-conversation. It is often missed because the client is quiet and not disruptive. A resting client can be awakened and follows a conversation, which separates normal rest from delirium. Pulling at lines is tempting because it is the classic picture of delirium, but it describes the hyperactive type.
questions.takeaway: Quiet withdrawal, slowed answers, and drifting off are hypoactive delirium, not rest.
questions.hintContent: Separate reduced activity with inattention from normal, easily interrupted rest.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA items about a subtype, choose only the findings that match that subtype.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client is admitted with new delirium. Once the client is safe and stable, which information should the nurse gather to help the team find the causes? Select all that apply.
options: When the client last seemed like their usual self, according to family.
Any new, stopped, or over-the-counter medicines, including sleep aids.
Recent food and fluid intake and urine and bowel elimination.
Alcohol or other substance use and the time of last use.
A plan to order every lab and imaging test linked to delirium for this client.
optionRationales: Correct. Baseline and time of onset are central to recognizing delirium.
Correct. Medicines are common triggers, and OTC sleep aids are often anticholinergic.
Correct. Dehydration, poor intake, and retention can trigger delirium.
Correct. Withdrawal is a possible cause that changes treatment.
Incorrect. Tests are chosen by the team from the history and findings, not ordered as a blanket routine.
questions.rationale: Delirium usually has more than one cause, so the nurse gathers baseline and onset, medicines including over-the-counter sleep aids, intake and elimination, and substance use. These data guide a clinician-directed workup. Ordering every listed test is tempting because it seems thorough, but tests are chosen by the team based on findings rather than run on every client. Good history often reveals several triggers at once.
questions.takeaway: Gather baseline, onset, medicines, intake, elimination, and substance use to find delirium triggers.
questions.hintContent: Think about what history could reveal a hidden trigger.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject options that replace clinical judgment with a blanket routine.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client is being treated for delirium caused by dehydration and a new opioid. His wife says he usually reads the paper, chats easily, and walks with a cane. Which findings indicate the client is improving? Select all that apply.
options: Follows a 10-minute conversation about the news without drifting off.
Sleeps at night and stays awake for most of the day.
Walks to the bathroom with his cane and standby help, with no falls.
Has been quiet and sleeping most of the day since a PRN sedative.
No longer calls out at night since wrist restraints were applied.
optionRationales: Correct. Sustained attention shows movement toward baseline.
Correct. A restored sleep-wake pattern is an expected outcome.
Correct. Function returning toward baseline without injury shows improvement.
Incorrect. Quiet after sedation may reflect oversedation, not recovery.
Incorrect. Less calling out under restraint shows restriction, not improved thinking.
questions.rationale: Recovery from delirium is judged by improved attention and alertness, function moving back toward baseline, a restored sleep-wake pattern, comfort, and no injury. Following a conversation, sleeping at night, and walking safely with his usual cane all show progress. A quiet day after a sedative is tempting to count as better, but reduced behavior may reflect oversedation. Silence under restraint shows only that movement is restricted.
questions.takeaway: Recovery means better attention and function toward baseline, not just quiet behavior.
questions.hintContent: Compare each finding with his wife’s description of his baseline.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, choose outcomes that show function, not outcomes caused by sedation or restraint.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client with hyperactive delirium is trying to get out of bed and pulling at the nasal cannula. The nurse has assessed oxygenation and pain. Which safety measures are appropriate at this time? Select all that apply.
options: Arrange continuous observation, such as a trained sitter.
Lower the bed, lock the wheels, and remove trip hazards.
Invite a familiar family member to stay if the client wishes.
Say who you are and use short sentences, one request at a time.
Apply bilateral wrist restraints as the first safety measure.
Close the door and leave the room dark so the client can calm down.
optionRationales: Correct. Close observation keeps the client safe without restraint.
Correct. Removing hazards reduces fall risk with the least restriction.
Correct. Familiar people can calm and orient the client.
Correct. Clear, concrete communication reduces fear and confusion.
Incorrect. Restraints are not first-line and can increase agitation and injury.
Incorrect. Isolation in a dark room removes cues and supervision.
questions.rationale: After assessing the physical causes, the nurse uses the least restrictive measures that keep the client safe. Continuous observation, a safe environment, familiar people, and clear simple communication reduce risk and distress. Wrist restraints are tempting because the client is pulling at oxygen, but restraints are not a default answer and can worsen agitation and injury. Leaving the client alone in a dark room removes both supervision and orienting cues.
questions.takeaway: Use supervision, a safe room, familiar people, and clear words before any restraint.
questions.hintContent: Ask which options protect the client without restricting movement.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the least restrictive effective options in safety SATA items.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A preceptor observes a new graduate nurse who has completed CAM training screening clients for delirium. Which actions by the new nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Follows the tool’s official steps for each feature.
Documents the behaviors seen, the time, and who provided the baseline.
Includes the screening result and any fluctuation in the handoff report.
Records a negative result from a quick impression during a conversation.
Treats a negative screen as proof delirium is absent despite an earlier decline.
optionRationales: Correct. Validated tools must be used with their official instructions.
Correct. Concrete documentation lets others follow the trend.
Correct. The next nurse needs to know what is new and what to watch.
Incorrect. A result must come from the tool, not a quick impression.
Incorrect. A negative screen does not erase an observed decline, because delirium fluctuates.
questions.rationale: The CAM is used by trained staff following its official steps, and a result should never be assigned from a quick impression. Good practice includes documenting observed behaviors, time, and the source of baseline, and passing the findings on in handoff. Treating a negative screen as final is tempting because it feels objective, but delirium fluctuates and a short interaction can miss it. Reassessment over time is essential.
questions.takeaway: Use the CAM as designed, document specifics, hand off changes, and reassess over time.
questions.hintContent: Ask which actions keep the screening valid and the trend visible.
questions.hintStrategy: In precepting SATA items, select the actions that follow the tool and protect continuity of care.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse admits an 84-year-old client for a bowel obstruction. Which factors in the client’s history increase the risk of developing delirium? Select all that apply.
options: Mild cognitive impairment diagnosed two years ago.
Severe hearing loss with hearing aids left at home.
Needs help with bathing and dressing at baseline.
Lives with a supportive spouse who visits daily.
Advanced age with several chronic diseases.
optionRationales: Correct. Existing cognitive impairment lowers brain reserve.
Correct. Sensory loss and missing aids increase delirium risk.
Correct. Prior functional limits are a known risk factor.
Incorrect. Family support is protective, not a risk factor.
Correct. Older age and chronic illness lower reserve.
questions.rationale: Risk factors such as older age, existing cognitive impairment, hearing or vision loss, severe or chronic illness, and prior functional limits lower the brain’s reserve. When a new trigger such as surgery, infection, or a new medicine is added, delirium becomes more likely. A supportive spouse is tempting to include because the item asks about the client’s situation, but family presence is protective. Identifying these risks on admission lets the nurse start prevention right away.
questions.takeaway: Older age, cognitive impairment, sensory loss, chronic illness, and functional limits raise delirium risk.
questions.hintContent: For each item, ask whether it lowers or protects the brain’s reserve.
questions.hintStrategy: In risk-factor SATA items, exclude options that are protective.
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
